notes.definition: DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides. Each nucleotide is a sugar and phosphate group with one of four bases (A, C, G or T) attached; a sequence of three bases codes for one amino acid, so the order of bases controls the order of amino acids in a protein.
explanation: DNA is a polymer made up of repeating units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and a phosphate group, with one of four different bases attached to the sugar. The four bases are given the letters A, C, G and T (you do not need to know their full names). In each long strand of DNA, sugar and phosphate sections alternate to form a backbone, and attached to each sugar is one of the four bases.

A DNA molecule has two strands that are held together by the bases, which pair up across the middle. The pairing is complementary: A on one strand is always linked to T on the opposite strand, and C is always linked to G. This means that if you know the base sequence of one strand, you can work out the other. It also means that in a DNA molecule the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of C equals the amount of G.

A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid. The order of the bases in a gene therefore controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a particular protein. A gene with 900 bases in its coding sequence codes for a protein of 300 amino acids. Different orders of bases give different orders of amino acids and so different proteins. (Higher tier) This is how the structure of DNA affects the protein made.

(Higher tier) Proteins are made (synthesised) on ribosomes in the cytoplasm. DNA cannot leave the nucleus, so a copy of the gene is made as a template molecule, which moves out of the nucleus to a ribosome. Carrier molecules each bring a specific amino acid to the ribosome, and the amino acids are added to the growing protein chain in the correct order, as set by the template. When the protein chain is complete, it folds up to form a unique shape. This unique shape enables the protein to do its job, for example as an enzyme, a hormone, or a structural protein such as collagen.

(Higher tier) Mutations are changes in the DNA base sequence and they occur continuously. Most mutations do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed. A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape. An enzyme may then no longer fit the substrate binding site (active site), or a structural protein may lose its strength.

(Higher tier) Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas may affect how genes are expressed. Genetic variants can therefore influence the phenotype either in coding DNA, by altering the activity of a protein, or in non-coding DNA, by altering how genes are expressed.
keyFacts: DNA is a polymer made of repeating nucleotide units.
A nucleotide is a sugar and a phosphate group with one of four bases attached to the sugar.
The four bases are A, C, G and T.
Each strand has alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with a base attached to each sugar.
Complementary pairs: A always pairs with T, C always pairs with G.
A sequence of three bases codes for one amino acid.
The order of bases controls the order of amino acids in a protein.
(HT) Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes using a template; carrier molecules bring specific amino acids in the correct order.
(HT) The completed chain folds into a unique shape that lets the protein work as an enzyme, hormone or structural protein such as collagen.
(HT) Most mutations have little or no effect; a few change the shape of a protein.
(HT) Non-coding DNA can switch genes on and off.

keyTerms.definition: The repeating unit of DNA: a sugar and a phosphate group with one of four bases attached to the sugar.
One of the four parts (A, C, G, T) attached to the sugars in DNA; their order carries the genetic code.
A on one strand always pairs with T on the other, and C always pairs with G.
A sequence of three bases that codes for one particular amino acid.
(HT) The structure in the cytoplasm where proteins are synthesised.
(HT) A copy of a gene that carries the base sequence from the nucleus to the ribosome.
(HT) A molecule that brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome to be added to the protein chain.
(HT) A change in the base sequence of DNA.
(HT) DNA that does not code for a protein; some of it switches genes on and off.

workedExamples.title: Writing the complementary strand
workedExamples.question: One strand of DNA has the base sequence A T T G C A G C. Write the sequence of the complementary strand.
steps: Use the pairing rules: A pairs with T, T with A, C with G and G with C.
Go along the strand one base at a time: A→T, T→A, T→A, G→C, C→G, A→T, G→C, C→G.
workedExamples.answer: T A A C G T C G

workedExamples.title: Bases and amino acids
workedExamples.question: A protein is made of 240 amino acids. What is the minimum number of bases needed in the gene to code for this protein?
steps: Three bases code for one amino acid.

workedExamples.title: Using base pairing to find percentages
workedExamples.question: In a sample of DNA, 22% of the bases are G. Calculate the percentage of A.
steps: G pairs with C, so C is also 22%.
A pairs with T, so A = 56 ÷ 2 = 28%.

workedExamples.title: (HT) Effect of a mutation
workedExamples.question: A mutation changes one base in the gene for an enzyme. Explain how this could stop the enzyme working.
steps: The change in base sequence may change a triplet, so a different amino acid is coded for.
The order of amino acids in the protein changes.
The protein chain may fold into a different shape, so the shape of the active site changes.
The substrate no longer fits the active site, so the enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction.
workedExamples.answer: The changed amino acid sequence changes the folding and the active site shape, so the substrate no longer fits.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a nucleotide is the same as a base.
misconceptions.right: In fact a nucleotide is a sugar plus a phosphate group plus one base. The base is only one part of it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think A pairs with G or C pairs with T.
misconceptions.right: In fact the pairs are always A with T and C with G.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think proteins are made in the nucleus.
misconceptions.right: (HT) In fact proteins are made on ribosomes in the cytoplasm. A copy of the gene carries the code out of the nucleus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think every mutation causes a disease.
misconceptions.right: (HT) In fact mutations happen continuously and most have no effect, or only a slight effect, on the protein. Only a few change its shape enough to change its function.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think DNA that does not code for proteins is useless.
misconceptions.right: (HT) In fact some non-coding DNA switches genes on and off, so changes in it can affect how genes are expressed.

realWorld: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutation that changes one base in the gene for haemoglobin, so one amino acid is different and the protein changes shape.
Collagen, a structural protein made by the method in this topic, gives strength to skin, tendons and bones; some inherited conditions are caused by mutations that weaken it.
Forensic scientists compare base sequences in non-coding regions of DNA, which vary greatly between people, to produce DNA profiles.
higherTier: Recall a simple description of protein synthesis: proteins are synthesised on ribosomes according to a template (a copy of the gene); carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing chain in the correct order.
When the protein chain is complete it folds into a unique shape, which enables it to do its job as an enzyme, a hormone or a structural protein such as collagen.
Explain simply how the structure of DNA affects the protein made, and how a change in DNA structure may result in a change in the protein synthesised by a gene.

Mutations occur continuously. Most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so its appearance or function is unchanged. A few code for an altered protein with a different shape: an enzyme may no longer fit its substrate binding site, or a structural protein may lose its strength.
Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts can switch genes on and off, so variations in them may affect how genes are expressed.
Genetic variants influence phenotype: in coding DNA by altering the activity of a protein, and in non-coding DNA by altering how genes are expressed.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): DNA structure (nucleotides, bases, complementary pairing, triplet code) and, for Higher tier, protein synthesis and mutations.
DNA is a polymer of repeating nucleotide units; each nucleotide is a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four bases (A, C, G, T) attached to the sugar.
Long strands of DNA have alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with a base attached to each sugar; C always links to G and T to A on the opposite strand.
A sequence of three bases codes for a particular amino acid; the order of bases controls the order of amino acids in a protein.
examTips: You will not be asked for the full names of the bases; use the letters A, T, C and G.
When describing a nucleotide, name all three parts: sugar, phosphate group and a base.

For mutation questions follow the chain: change in base sequence → change in amino acid sequence → protein folds differently → different shape → enzyme active site no longer fits substrate (or structural protein weaker).
For bases to amino acids calculations, divide the number of bases by 3; for amino acids to bases, multiply by 3.
If a question says 'most mutations', remember they have little or no effect on the protein.
summary: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides: sugar + phosphate + one base (A, C, G or T).
Sugar and phosphate alternate along each strand; bases attach to sugars.
A pairs with T and C pairs with G.
Three bases code for one amino acid; base order sets amino acid order.
(HT) Proteins are made on ribosomes using a template; carrier molecules bring amino acids.
(HT) The chain folds into a unique shape for its function.
(HT) Most mutations have little effect; some change a protein's shape and function.
(HT) Non-coding DNA can switch genes on and off.

questions.question: What is the name of the repeating unit that makes up DNA?
markScheme: 1 mark: nucleotide
questions.explanation: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides. Amino acids are the units of proteins, glucose of starch, and fatty acids are part of lipids.

questions.question: Which base always pairs with A in DNA?
markScheme: 1 mark: T
questions.explanation: The complementary pairs are A with T and C with G.

questions.question: Which of these is part of a nucleotide?
markScheme: 1 mark: a phosphate group
questions.explanation: Each nucleotide has a sugar, a phosphate group and one base. Ribosomes make proteins and amino acids are the units of proteins.

questions.question: How many bases code for one amino acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3
questions.explanation: A sequence of three bases codes for a particular amino acid.

questions.question: One DNA strand has the sequence C G A T T C. What is the sequence on the complementary strand?
options: G C A T T G
C G A T T C
G C T A A G
T A G C C T
markScheme: 1 mark: G C T A A G
questions.explanation: Pair each base: C→G, G→C, A→T, T→A, T→A, C→G. The other options either copy the strand or use incorrect pairs.

questions.question: What makes up the 'backbone' of each strand of DNA?
options: Amino acids joined in a chain
markScheme: 1 mark: alternating sugar and phosphate sections
questions.explanation: Sugar and phosphate alternate along each strand. The bases are attached to the sugars and point inwards to pair with bases on the other strand.

questions.question: How does the order of bases in a gene affect the protein made?
options: It controls the order in which amino acids are assembled
It controls how many ribosomes there are
It controls the number of chromosomes
It controls the amount of sugar in the cell
markScheme: 1 mark: it controls the order in which amino acids are assembled
questions.explanation: Every three bases code for one amino acid, so the base order decides the amino acid order, which decides the protein.

questions.question: (Higher) Where in a cell are proteins synthesised?
markScheme: 1 mark: on ribosomes
questions.explanation: Proteins are made on ribosomes in the cytoplasm. The gene stays in the nucleus, so a copy (template) is sent out.

questions.question: (Higher) What is the job of carrier molecules in protein synthesis?
options: To copy the gene in the nucleus
To bring specific amino acids to the ribosome in the correct order
To fold the protein into its shape
To carry the finished protein out of the cell
markScheme: 1 mark: to bring specific amino acids to the ribosome in the correct order
questions.explanation: Each carrier molecule brings a specific amino acid, matched to the template, so the amino acids are added in the right order.

questions.question: (Higher) A mutation occurs in a gene but the protein produced is unchanged. Which is the best explanation?
options: Most mutations do not alter the protein, or alter it only slightly
The mutation was in the ribosome
markScheme: 1 mark: most mutations do not alter the protein or alter it only slightly
questions.explanation: Mutations occur continuously and most have no effect, or only a slight effect, on the protein's appearance or function.

questions.question: (Higher) A mutation occurs in non-coding DNA close to a gene. What is the most likely effect?
options: It changes the order of amino acids in the protein
It always stops the cell dividing
It may change whether the gene is switched on or off
It has no possible effect because non-coding DNA does nothing
markScheme: 1 mark: it may change whether the gene is switched on or off
questions.explanation: Non-coding DNA does not code for amino acids, but some of it switches genes on and off, so a variant here can alter how the gene is expressed.

questions.question: Name the three parts of a nucleotide.
markScheme: 1 mark: sugar
1 mark: phosphate (group)
1 mark: base (A, C, G or T)
questions.explanation: A nucleotide is a common sugar and a phosphate group with one of four bases attached to the sugar.

questions.question: State the base pairs found in DNA.
markScheme: 1 mark: A pairs with T
1 mark: C pairs with G
questions.explanation: These are the complementary base pairs. They are always the same.

questions.question: Describe how the structure of DNA carries the code for making a protein.
markScheme: 1 mark: a sequence of three bases codes for a particular amino acid
1 mark: the order of bases controls the order of amino acids in the protein
questions.explanation: The genetic code is read in threes; the order of these triplets sets the order of amino acids.

questions.question: (Higher) Describe how a protein is synthesised in a cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: a copy of the gene (template) is made and moves from the nucleus to a ribosome
1 mark: carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to the ribosome
1 mark: amino acids are joined in the order set by the template / chain folds into a unique shape when complete
questions.explanation: This is the simple description required: template to ribosome, carrier molecules bring amino acids in the correct order, chain then folds.

questions.question: (Higher) A mutation changes one base in the gene for an enzyme. Explain how this may result in the enzyme no longer working.
markScheme: 1 mark: a different amino acid may be coded for / amino acid sequence changes
1 mark: the protein folds into a different shape
1 mark: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits (binds)
questions.explanation: The chain of cause and effect is: base change → amino acid change → different folding → different active site shape → substrate does not fit.

questions.question: (Higher) Explain why the final shape of a protein is important. Give an example in your answer.
acceptedAnswers: enables it to do its job
markScheme: 1 mark: the unique shape enables the protein to do its job
1 mark: example, for example an enzyme's active site fits its substrate / a hormone fits its receptor / collagen's shape gives strength
questions.explanation: Proteins fold into unique shapes, and their function depends on that shape: enzymes, hormones and structural proteins such as collagen.

questions.question: (Higher) Describe two ways in which genetic variants can influence the phenotype.
markScheme: 1 mark: variants in coding DNA can alter the activity of a protein
1 mark: variants in non-coding DNA can alter how genes are expressed (switched on or off)
questions.explanation: These are the two routes given in the specification: changing a protein itself, or changing whether and how much a gene is expressed.

questions.question: (Higher) A mutation in the gene for collagen produces collagen with a slightly different shape. Suggest the effect this could have on the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: the collagen (structural protein) may lose its strength
1 mark: so tissues such as skin, bones or tendons may be weaker / damaged more easily
questions.explanation: The specification states that a structural protein with a different shape may lose its strength.

questions.question: A gene is 600 bases long and all of it codes for a protein. How many amino acids are in the protein?
questions.explanation: Three bases code for one amino acid, so divide the number of bases by 3.

questions.question: A protein contains 412 amino acids. What is the minimum number of bases in the gene that codes for it?
questions.explanation: Each amino acid needs three bases: 412 × 3 = 1236.

questions.question: In a sample of DNA, 30% of the bases are T. Calculate the percentage of bases that are C.
markScheme: 1 mark: A = 30% so A + T = 60%
questions.explanation: T pairs with A, so A is also 30%. That leaves 40% for C and G, which are equal: 20% each.

questions.question: A section of double-stranded DNA contains 1000 bases in total. 220 of the bases are G. Calculate the number of A bases.
markScheme: 1 mark: C = 220, so G + C = 440
questions.explanation: G pairs with C, so there are 220 C. That leaves 560 bases shared equally between A and T: 280 each.

questions.question: A gene contains 1350 bases. Only 40% of the bases code for amino acids. How many amino acids are in the protein made?
markScheme: 1 mark: coding bases = 0.40 × 1350 = 540
questions.explanation: Find the number of coding bases first, then divide by three. 0.4 × 1350 = 540, and 540 ÷ 3 = 180.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
markScheme: Indicative content: DNA is a polymer; made of repeating nucleotide units; each nucleotide is a sugar, a phosphate group and one of four bases; base attached to the sugar; four bases A, C, G and T; each strand has alternating sugar and phosphate sections; two strands; bases pair: A with T and C with G (complementary); two strands form a double helix; sequence of three bases codes for an amino acid.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a detailed and accurate description including nucleotides with all three parts, the sugar-phosphate backbone and complementary base pairing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example that DNA has two strands and four bases.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Build up from the smallest unit: nucleotide (sugar, phosphate, base), then strand (alternating sugar and phosphate), then two strands joined by complementary base pairs, twisted into a double helix.

questions.question: (Higher) Explain how the sequence of bases in a gene determines the function of the protein it codes for, and how a mutation in the gene might affect that function.
markScheme: Indicative content: three bases code for one amino acid; order of bases determines order of amino acids; a copy of the gene (template) goes to a ribosome; carrier molecules bring specific amino acids in the correct order; amino acids joined into a chain; chain folds into a unique shape; shape determines function, for example enzyme active site fits substrate, hormone, collagen strength. Mutation: change in base sequence; most mutations do not alter the protein or alter it only slightly, so function unchanged; a few change an amino acid and the protein folds into a different shape; an enzyme may no longer fit its substrate binding site; a structural protein may lose strength; mutations in non-coding DNA may affect whether the gene is switched on or off.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, detailed explanation linking base sequence to amino acid order, protein synthesis and folding to function, and explaining both that most mutations have little effect and how some change shape and function.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links base order to amino acid order and protein shape, with some reference to how a mutation could affect function.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example that genes code for proteins and mutations change them.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: This question tests the full Higher tier chain: base sequence → amino acid sequence (via template, ribosome and carrier molecules) → folding → unique shape → function, and how altering the first step may (or may not) alter the last.

questions.question: (Higher) Which protein is a structural protein named in the specification as an example of how a protein's shape lets it do its job?
markScheme: 1 mark: collagen
questions.explanation: Collagen is a structural protein. Amylase is an enzyme and insulin is a hormone, which are the other types of protein mentioned. Haemoglobin is a transport protein.

questions.question: How many different bases are found in DNA?
markScheme: 1 mark: four
questions.explanation: The four bases are A, C, G and T.
